title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Page 4 of a typescript on elliptic curves over a base S. It continues a construction of the Weierstrass equation and the standard invariants of an elliptic curve, written in the style of Deligne's 'Formulaire d'après Tate'.

Setting from page 3. E/S is an elliptic curve with zero section e and ω = e*Ω¹. Fix an invertible section π of ω. Zariski-locally there are sections x ∈ p_*O(2e) and y ∈ p_*O(3e) with polar parts π^{-2} and -π^{-3} respectively.

Existence and uniqueness of the equation (1.3) via (1.1), i.e. Riemann–Roch rank counting. Both sides of (1.3) are viewed as sections of p_*O(6e). By the normalisation, y² and x³ have the same leading polar term, so y² - x³ lies in p_*O(5e). The monomials xy, x², y, x, 1 lie in O(5e), O(4e), O(3e), O(2e), O(0) respectively. They therefore form a basis adapted to the pole filtration, and y² - x³ has a unique expansion in them with coefficients a_i. This is the standard proof that a Weierstrass equation exists and is unique once (x, y) are fixed.

Invariant differential. With F = y² + a1xy + a3y - x³ - a2x² - a4x - a6, the invariant differential is π = dx/F_y = -dy/F_x = dx/(2y + a1x + a3) = dy/(3x² + 2a2x + a4 - a1y).

Converse. Any equation (1.3) defines a plane cubic of genus 1 with a flex at (0:1:0) whose inflectional tangent is the line at infinity. (Implicitly one needs Δ invertible for this.)

Invariants (1.4). Tate's b2, b4, b6, b8, together with two less standard quantities:
- d6 = b2b4 - 18b6
- d8 = b2²b4 - 48b4² + 18b2b6
The stated identities are -4b8 = b4² - b2b6, 12d6 = c6 + b2c4 and -12d8 = c4² + b2c6, with c4, c6 from (1.5) on the next page.

Purpose. Given the title (Gauss–Manin, Picard–Fuchs, Cartier operator), d6 and d8 are clearly prepared for computing the Gauss–Manin connection / Kodaira–Spencer derivation on the coefficients. Under x ↦ x + r, b2 shifts like a quasi-modular weight-2 form: u²b2' = b2 + 12r, an analogue of E2. Page 5 gives u⁶d6' = d6 + c4r and u⁸d8' = d8 - c6r. So d6 and d8 are, up to normalisation and sign, the Ramanujan/Serre-type derivatives of c4 and c6, matching θE4 ∝ E2E4 - E6 and θE6 ∝ E2E6 - E4². In other words, they are the algebraic, Weierstrass-coefficient form of the Ramanujan differential system as it arises from Gauss–Manin. This is the material of Katz's work on the Gauss–Manin connection and modular forms (1973).
errors:
No mathematical errors found. Every identity was checked by expansion:
- -b8 matches Tate's b8 = a1²a6 + 4a2a6 - a1a3a4 + a2a3² - a4².
- 4b8 = b2b6 - b4².
- c6 + b2c4 = 12b2b4 - 216b6 = 12d6.
- c4² + b2c6 = -12(b2²b4 - 48b4² + 18b2b6) = -12d8.
- -dy/F_x equals dy/(3x² + 2a2x + a4 - a1y).
Minor gap: the converse statement ('toute équation (1.3) est l'équation d'une courbe de genre 1') tacitly requires the discriminant Δ to be invertible; Δ is only defined on the next page.
Minor sign convention: y has polar part -π^{-3}, so the sign of π depends on this choice. This is consistent with dx/F_y but differs in sign from some other conventions.

ideas.what: Existence and uniqueness of the Weierstrass equation via the pole-order filtration of p_*O(ne) over a general base S
ideas.modern_name: Weierstrass model of an elliptic curve over a base scheme (Riemann–Roch argument)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Weierstrass); relative version in Tate's formulary as written up by Deligne (1975), and Katz–Mazur
ideas.where_published: Deligne, 'Courbes elliptiques: formulaire (d'après J. Tate)', LNM 476 (1975); Katz–Mazur (1985)

ideas.modern_name: Invariant (Néron) differential of a Weierstrass equation

ideas.what: Tate's quantities b2, b4, b6, b8 and the relation 4b8 = b2b6 - b4²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Tate (circulated ca. 1965-68), written up by Deligne 1975

ideas.what: Auxiliary invariants d6 = (c6 + b2c4)/12 and d8 = -(c4² + b2c6)/12, which transform affinely under x ↦ x + r (d6 ↦ d6 + c4r, d8 ↦ d8 - c6r)
ideas.modern_name: Algebraic form of the Ramanujan/Serre derivatives of c4 and c6 (quasi-modular combinations with b2 playing the role of E2); input to the Gauss–Manin connection on the Weierstrass family
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan (the differential system); Katz 1973 (Gauss–Manin and the Serre θ-operator algebraically); later Movasati's 'Gauss–Manin connection in disguise'
ideas.where_published: Katz, 'p-adic properties of modular schemes and modular forms' (LNM 350, 1973), in spirit; the explicit d6 and d8 notation I cannot place in a published source (unsure)

missed.claim: The typescript introduces named quantities d6 and d8 in Tate-style b-coordinates, with explicit affine transformation laws under the change of coordinates (1.2). These are essentially the coordinate-level Ramanujan derivatives that later reappear (e.g. in Movasati's quasi-modular/Gauss–Manin work) without, to my knowledge, this notation. This is a minor presentational detail of a known circle of ideas (Katz 1973), not a new result.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical interest. It documents that the algebraic Ramanujan system over an arbitrary base (including characteristic 2 and 3, via the b-coordinates) was being worked out in the Gauss–Manin/Cartier context around 1972. The authorship is probably Deligne or Katz rather than Grothendieck.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a standard Tate/Deligne formulary page. The only non-standard element is the d6, d8 invariants with quasi-modular transformation laws. These are a Weierstrass-coordinate rendering of the Ramanujan derivatives tied to Gauss–Manin, which is well known in substance (Katz 1973). The text is likely not by Grothendieck himself.
transcription_corrections: The image confirms 'p_*O(6e)' (the '6' is slightly blurred), 'π' for the invariant differential, and 'd_8 = b_2² b_4 - 2⁴·3 b_4² + 2·3² b_2 b_6', i.e. coefficients 48 and 18; the machine transcription renders the last as '2 3^2', meaning 2·3².
The calligraphic O in the typescript is a hand-drawn script O; the transcription \mathcal{O} is correct.
